# R338 — pristine upstream bench.sh long-row semantics

Date: 2026-10-13 (JST). Read-only source audit of /home/yayoi/ghq/github.com/Niko1221/Strata/.worktree/bench-upstream-v0143-pristine-20261012 at HEAD 7695859aa13afb248bdb4d36f9b2e95707db079d. Reviewed pristine bench.sh, tools/strata_bench.py, relevant server timing semantics, and registry v180 metadata (860 completed reports). No model/server/process/test/build/GPU/profiler/import/Git-mutation/cleanup action was taken. The prepared quiet server config and source guard result were not changed. No benchmark was run, so this is a source interpretation only.

Source hashes:
- bench.sh: 7091b38069a62ec315043d720a3e2f98cc82216a3ba4fe72790764fea49db963
- tools/strata_bench.py: 818bbba34a288023545843a96d56c679079beed55821cc85eaa343f156202f3b

## What --long measures

The upstream client calibrates token-per-word from two small chat requests containing 200 and 800 words, then estimates the fixed template/tag overhead. It constructs each target prompt as a generated word list sized from that slope. --long adds run_prompt(32768, "32K"): three fresh HTTP chat prompts by default, each with max_tokens=24, temperature 0, and thinking disabled. The suite refuses to schedule 4K/16K/32K when the configured context is smaller than requested input + 24 output + 256 margin. The long prompt is run after short chat, 4K, 16K and agent tests, in the same suite order.

The request's target is approximately 32,768 input tokens, not an exact fixed token sequence. Word-count calibration and template/tokenization mean the generated prompt can land above or below target. Use each result's observed prompt_tokens; do not quote 32,768 as an achieved count. The exact-context minimum check is 33,048, so a context of exactly 32,768 skips the test. A 32K row should be called a roughly-32K fresh-prompt result only if it ran and its observed prompt_tokens support that description.

For each request, digest records prompt_tokens from usage, cached/reused tokens from usage details or engine timing, read_tokens from engine prompt_n (or prompt_tokens minus cached when prompt_n is absent), prompt_tps from engine prompt_per_second, and TTFT from the client's first nonempty streamed content/reasoning piece. In this server revision prompt_n is the count actually read, not all prompt tokens: request_timings subtracts cached/session-resident tokens, and prompt_per_second is prompt_n divided by prompt_ms. Therefore actual total prompt_tokens, read_tokens, reused_tokens, and prompt_tps answer different questions. The report's fresh-prompt table prints actual prompt tokens and reused tokens, but not read_tokens; per-request results.json contains read_tokens. Check all three before interpreting a row. A unique leading bench tag is intended to prevent full prompt-cache reuse, but measured reused_tokens is the evidence; shared template/prefix or session-resident tokens can still affect the count.

## Decode numbers and summaries

The 24-token limit makes --long primarily a long-prefill / first-token test, not a sustained long-context decode benchmark. The streamed response can finish before the cap, so inspect each generated_tokens value rather than assuming 24 decode tokens. digest calculates per-request decode_tps from engine predicted_per_second when present, or a client-wall-clock fallback when it is absent. For fresh prompts run_prompt stores the complete digest for each request in results.json, so a per-request decode_tps may be present. However, the prompts aggregate stores only prompt_tps, TTFT, prompt_tokens and reused_tokens; summary_metrics and the README/console summary omit prompt-row decode_tps and display the cap as “24” generated tokens. Do not infer an aggregate 32K decode rate from the console/README, and do not report the output cap as observed generation. If long-context decode is required, the pristine client does not provide a long decode phase; use the short chat or agent-turn decode summaries only as separate workloads, and do not silently modify upstream client code.

The engine timings are preferable for prompt/decode rate. Client-measured TTFT includes HTTP, stream and server overhead until the first nonempty content/reasoning delta. Temperature 0 and disabled thinking reduce variance, but the short 24-token output still makes the decode rate sensitive to first-token handling, stop behavior and token count. TTFT and prompt throughput should be the primary interpretation of --long.

## Repeats, tags, and across-arm comparison

Default runs=3. They are three fresh requests, summarized with median, minimum, maximum and n; this is a small variability screen, not a tight confidence interval. Prompt run tags contain run index and requested size plus a Suite nonce derived from current Unix seconds. The generated word-list body is the same construction, but run tags and nonce make the actual token strings differ. Consequently, pristine --long provides comparable fresh workload shape and cache exclusion, not exact prompt-by-prompt paired timing across arms. Each separate invocation creates its own nonce; retain each arm's actual prompt_tokens/read/reused counts and medians/ranges. Do not claim a paired identical-input benchmark from the client.

To compare several implementation arms, use the identical pristine bench.sh/strata_bench.py source and invocation settings against each arm's own quiet server, one request at a time (no --clients), with --long and the default three runs. Keep model/quant, context, server config aside from the intended variable, device, power/background condition, prompt settings and runtime fixed. Run client arms serially or alternate arm order across repeats to reduce thermal/order bias; the client itself does not randomize or counterbalance arms. Save exact command, commit/config/source hashes and server logs outside the client output if they are not captured by results.json. The result's params.command string omits some options such as --url, --config, --api-key, --out and --port, so do not rely on it alone to prove the actual invocation. Pristine code must remain unchanged for every arm.

## What the other rows mean

Short chat is three fixed short questions, each run three times, up to 100 output tokens. Its decode and TTFT characterize short-request interactive behavior; it says little about prefill at 32K.

The agent test is six turns per session (initial system/tools request plus five follow-ups), repeated three sessions by default, with each follow-up adding roughly 1,500 words and the model's prior answer. It is useful as a client-style conversation-cache workload: report reused/read token counts and TTFT per turn, along with the summary cache hit/reread/new-token metrics. It is not a 32K prompt test. The agent file content is taken from the checked-out README/docs when those files are long enough, otherwise generated filler. Across different worktrees/revisions those document texts can differ, so agent timing/cache deltas are auxiliary unless the exact content is confirmed common. The agent summary's decode rate is across follow-up turns, not a 32K decode rate.

4K and 16K fresh prompts provide useful scaling context with the same output cap and client logic. Their measured token counts matter for the same reasons as 32K. --clients is optional burst throughput and latency; it changes the workload and should be left off for a single-request per-arm comparison. The user-requested quiet server config should stay the same except for the one experimental server option being assessed.

## Safe claim language and limits

A successful run can support a claim such as “with pristine upstream bench.sh at this exact commit, three fresh prompts of X/Y/Z observed tokens produced median engine prompt rate P tok/s and median client TTFT F s; engine-reported read/reuse counts were ...”. It cannot support “exactly 32K”, “sustained 32K decode”, “same prompt paired across arms”, “cache-free” without checking reuse counts, or an accuracy/quality claim. Upstream documentation explicitly labels these prompts “about” the target and calls the result speed-only, with no correctness check.

Current status from the task handoff remains: CPU help and pristine-source guard passed elsewhere; the actual model benchmark has not run. This report neither authorizes nor supplies its result.
